title: Fire
hookLine: a monk cuts a hole in a perfectly good mat and hangs it in front of a fire. why?
tomorrow: how do you look at something you can't see?

lines: A CIRCLE OF FRIENDS GOES QUIET.
A MAT WITH A HOLE IN IT.
cards: Birthday candles get a few seconds of attention before somebody blows them out. A campfire gets longer: a whole circle of friends goes quiet, phones down, watching nothing but the flame.
An old meditation manual, Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, takes that stare and turns it into a practice, and it begins with a strange bit of craft. A monk splits damp wood and lets it dry.
He builds a fire in a sheltered spot. Then he takes a mat, or a piece of leather, or cloth, cuts a round hole in it, and hangs it between himself and the fire. He sits down facing the hole.
Why ruin a perfectly good mat?

teach.b: Because the hole is a frame. Buddhaghosa is precise about what to leave out.

teach.h: NOT THE STICKS, NOT THE SMOKE.
teach.b: Not the grass and sticks at the bottom, where the fire is fed. Not the smoke curling off the top. Take the thick middle of the flame, he says, and stay there.
Don't dwell on its color or its heat. Hold only the name: fire. Tejo, in Pali.
What comes next comes in stages.

teach.h: RESTLESS, THEN STILL, LIKE RED CLOTH.
teach.b: At first the image is restless, like bits of flame breaking off and dropping away.
With patience a steadier sign can appear, and his pictures for it are lovely: a piece of red cloth hanging still in space, a golden fan, a golden column. Then a surprising aside.
Someone who did this practice before, in an earlier life as the tradition tells it, may need no mat at all. A lamp flame, a fire in an oven, a forest burning in the distance can be enough.
Now notice what the mat doesn't do. It doesn't put the fire out or clear away the smoke. The sticks are still crackling.

teach.h: THE NOISE STAYS. IT'S NOT THE OBJECT.
teach.b: Everything else is still there; it just isn't the object.
That's the craft: not fighting the noise, but choosing a frame and resting inside it.

how: In Theravada meditation the fire kasina is taken up with a teacher's guidance, using a flame seen through a round hole in a screen, as Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga describes it.

o: a ritual offering burned to honor the Buddha
a flame framed by a screen, held as a meditation object
a test of courage, sitting close to flames unafraid

games.q: what's in the frame — tap the pairs.

s: meditation means getting rid of every distraction first
the mat leaves the sticks and smoke where they are. it only frames the middle of the flame.
Buddhaghosa says to focus on the flame's heat
he says to leave its color and heat alone and hold the plain name: fire.
the steadier sign is pictured as red cloth hanging still in space
or a golden fan, or a golden column.

games.q: a group call: five people talking at once, and you're the one taking notes. what would the monk's mat do here?
o: ask everyone to go quiet, and start writing only when the call is calm.
pick the one thread that matters and follow it; let the rest run on.
write down every word anyone says, so that nothing gets lost.
games.why: the mat never puts the fire out. it frames the one part worth watching and lets the rest be.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe to light, light it; if not, a lamp or any small glow will do. Let your eyes rest on the bright middle, not the wick and not what rises above it.
When your mind drifts, say fire, quietly, and come back to the middle.

wordCard.voice: Fire: tejo in Pali. A flame seen through a hole in a screen, so its bright middle is all there is to look at.

orig.note: Pali: fire, heat. In Buddhaghosa's telling, the plain name held in mind while gazing at the flame.

carryVoice: Your line: the flame. The sticks and the smoke can stay; they're just outside the frame. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the fire kasina: dry wood, a screen of mat, leather or cloth with a round hole; leave aside the grass and sticks below and the smoke above; take the sign in the dense middle of the flame; not its color or heat, but the name 'fire'; the learning sign like flame breaking off, the counterpart sign motionless like red cloth in space, a gold fan, a gold column; one with past practice may need only a lamp flame, an oven fire or a forest fire)
